# What the field looks like

Four things are in your notes. A gene record from Chapter 5, a hit table from
Chapter 7, a tree from Chapter 19, a results table from Chapter 24. Every one
of them came out of a browser tab, and that's one path through a field that has
several. Two people can hold the same job title and spend their weeks on work
the other one couldn't name. So what are the other paths, and where does the
nearest one start?

## Six questions, and the four you've already asked

A subfield is easier to recognize by the question it asks than by the software
it runs. The alignment step from Chapter 18 turns up in genomics and again in
phylogenetics. The two questions stay separate.

**Genomics.** What sequence is in this sample, and what differs between this
one and that one? You started here in Chapter 5, and the whole of Part 4 is
that question asked of twelve mouse samples at once. Where the molecule is RNA
rather than DNA, the work gets filed under transcriptomics. One person often
does both inside a week.

**Phylogenetics.** Which of these came from which ancestor, and in what order
did the lineages split? Chapter 19. You built a tree of one gene across five
species and it put the mouse next to the chicken, confidently, with no warning
attached. The answer is a claim about history, and history doesn't re-run.

**Structural biology.** What shape does this protein fold into, and which part
of it touches what? You did it in Chapter 8. A crystal structure deposited in
2001 sat on your screen next to a model computed in 2025. One of those is a
measurement. The other is a prediction that ships with a confidence score for
every residue, and Chapter 8 showed you where to read it.

**Systems biology.** How do the parts behave together, and can you predict what
the whole does? You did one section of it in Chapter 25. You took your gene
list and asked which curated groups of genes it landed in more often than
chance allows. A gene set is the small end of the idea. The large end builds a model
that produces a number you can hold against a measurement.

**Single cell.** The four above ask about a sample. This one asks what each
cell in that sample is doing, and how many kinds of cell were in the tube to
start with. You haven't done it. Your own table has twelve columns where a
single cell experiment would have thousands.

**Drug discovery.** Which molecule binds this protein, and what happens to the
cell when it does? Testing a molecule against a protein on a computer needs a
structure to test it against, so this one opens on the question Chapter 8 left
you holding. How much of that structure do you believe? You haven't done this
one either.

::: {.why}
Nobody polices these borders. The tree you built in Chapter 19 came out of
sequences retrieved the Chapter 5 way, lined up in columns of the kind
Chapter 18 taught you to read. It still counts as phylogenetics. Papers from
two of these subfields will open on the same shape of table: rows for things,
columns for conditions. Joining either one to a second file means deciding
which identifier maps to which, which is the morning Chapter 2 described. What
carries across a border with you is smaller than the subject matter. You know a
count needs a denominator. You know an identifier isn't an identity. Those two
are what make a methods section in an unfamiliar subfield readable at all.
:::

## One table, four of those questions

Load your own count matrix one more time, and count what's in the whole of it
rather than in one row.

```{python}
import pandas as pd

counts = pd.read_csv("data/GSE60450_counts.tsv.gz", sep="\t")
sample_cols = list(counts.columns[2:])
zeros = (counts[sample_cols] == 0).sum().sum()
total = counts[sample_cols].size

print("genes (rows):  ", counts.shape[0])
print("samples (cols):", len(sample_cols))
print("numbers in all:", total)
print("of those, zero:", zeros)
print("percent zero:  ", round(100 * zeros / total, 1))
```

A third of that table is zero, and every column in it is a pool of many cells.
Now put four of the six questions to it.

Genomics asked which rows moved between the groups, and Chapter 24 answered
that. Single cell keeps the rows and replaces the twelve columns with
thousands, one per cell. A run of the same size spreads its reads across all of
them, so most entries land on zero. A gene that reads as absent in one cell may
only be unobserved there, and the two look identical in the table.

Systems biology asks which of the moved rows connect to each other, and it
takes the connections from a database somebody else assembled. Drug discovery
asks whether anything on your list is worth binding, which sends you back to
Chapter 8 for a structure.

::: {.check}
Your first two numbers should be 27,179 and 12. That's the whole file, before
any filtering. The filter in Chapter 24 built a second table of 14,210 rows by
dropping the genes too quiet to test. If that's the number you see, this cell
read something other than `data/GSE60450_counts.tsv.gz`. Both counts are right
about different tables, which is the Chapter 5 lesson turning up again in
Part 5.
:::

## Three jobs that all get called bioinformatics

Titles move around more than the work does, so here are the three shapes
underneath, described by what a week holds.

**Research scientist.** The question is yours. You decide what's worth
measuring and then argue for it in writing, so more of the week goes on prose
than a beginner expects. Papers, and the sections of grant applications nobody
else will write. Code is a means here, and plenty of it gets written to run
once. What you're buying is authority over the question, and the other two
roles trade that away. Where a doctorate is required, the posting says so.

**Bioinformatics analyst.** Somebody else brings the question and the data,
often in a state you wouldn't have chosen. The week is pipelines and metadata
archaeology, plus telling a biologist whether the result is real or the samples
got swapped. The same analysis runs many times over, so reproducibility stops
being a virtue and turns into how you survive Thursday. Whoever hires for this
reads your application for one thing: evidence you can take a messy dataset to
a defensible answer. That evidence is what Chapter 26 asked you to publish.

**Software engineer on biological tools.** Your users are the other two. You
build what they run, so the week is code review, tests, issue triage, and a
release that must not break somebody's paper. You need enough biology to know
what a column means, and less of it than the other two need. Work here is
visible from outside before anybody meets you, because the repository is
public. That's where Chapter 28 sends you to file your first issue.

::: {.trap}
You filter job listings by title. The same job goes up as bioinformatics
scientist in one place and computational biologist in another, and two postings
under one title can want two different weeks. Search a single word, read a thin
page of results, decide the work isn't there for somebody like you: nothing
errored, and the conclusion is wrong. Chapter 2 had you open a job board and
search all three field names. Read the duties paragraph and let the heading go.
:::

## How people get in

Three routes, and this book has been walking one of them the whole time.

The traditional one is a degree. A master's or a doctorate buys supervised time
and a thesis with somebody's signature under yours. It costs years and usually
money. It's also the only route that satisfies a posting whose first
requirement line names the degree.

The second is a sideways move. People arrive from a biology degree with no
code, or from code with no biology, and pick up the missing half while being
paid for the half they brought. Chapter 1 gave you the closest thing to a
measurement of that: in two surveys of working practitioners, 76 percent and
64 percent called their bioinformatics skills self-taught.

The third is the slow public one, and you're already on it. You do the work
where it can be read: a reproduced figure from Chapter 27, a documentation fix
from Chapter 28, a notebook from Chapter 26 that a stranger can open and run.
Nobody grants you this route and nobody can take it back. Nobody announces the
end of it either. Your artifacts do the job a certificate would otherwise do,
so they have to be finished ones.

Free structured material exists for all three routes, and Chapter 30 lists it.
Every entry there names what the resource is bad at, which is the field no
resource page prints about itself.

Neither question may be answerable from the count matrix on your disk. If one
of them is, you've rewritten the genomics question in fresh words and it's
still asking which rows moved. A systems question has to name something outside
your table, a pathway or a partner protein. A drug discovery question has to
name a structure, and Chapter 8 is where you find out whether one exists for
your gene.
:::

## If it breaks

::: {.ifbreaks}
::: {.errfix err="FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'data/GSE60450_counts.tsv.gz'"}
Python is speaking, and it's telling you nothing sits at the path you handed
it. Colab throws the whole folder away when the runtime recycles, so a session
you left open since Chapter 24 no longer has the file next to it. This is the
same break as the one in Chapter 20, and the cure is the same: list the current
folder's contents before you retype the path.
:::

::: {.errfix err="Every posting you read wants a doctorate"}
You searched one word. Duties are what separate the three roles above, and a
title is what a search box matches on, so one query returns one flavor of job.
Read the duties paragraph before the requirements list. Duties like "design
studies and publish" belong to the first role above. The other two get
advertised under words you haven't tried. Where the requirement line really is
there, Chapter 28's rule holds and it means what it says.
:::

::: {.errfix err="You open a methods section in a new subfield and none of the nouns are familiar"}
The nouns change per subfield and the shape doesn't. Find the four steps from
Chapter 9: what got retrieved, what got compared, what got judged, what got
annotated against a coordinate. Sentences that fit none of the four are the
part of the paper that's new, and they're the ones worth looking up.
:::
:::
